Sadism is enjoying someone else's pain.

Two of the four stood out. In both studies, people higher on psychopathy and sadism reported more support for Israeli violence and more support for Hamas violence. Not one or the other. Both. The pattern held when Greitemeyer accounted for where people sat politically, so it was not party feeling in disguise. Narcissism did not behave this way — it was tied to support for Hamas violence in the second study, and nothing else. Machiavellianism was tied to neither.

The second study also asked why. It tested two bridges: interest in militarism, meaning a fascination with weapons, special forces and martial arts; and moral disengagement, the mental tricks people use to justify harm so they never feel guilty. Both partly explained the link to support for Israeli violence. Neither explained the link to Hamas violence at all.

That gap is the honest result. If one mechanism were doing the work, it should have worked on both sides. It did not. So the road from trait to judgement is not the same road for each actor, and nobody yet knows what the other road is.

The finding is two pictures laid over each other. Most of what predicts support for political violence is still political: whose side you are on, who you count as the victim. Under that, in some people, sits something that does not check the flag first.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Two online studies. The first: 257 German speakers, mostly in Austria and Germany. The second: 470 UK citizens. Each person filled in a standard Dark Tetrad questionnaire, reported their political orientation, and rated their support for violent actions by Israel and by Hamas.

Ordinary patterns showed up too. Older people backed Israeli actions more and Hamas actions less. Men reported more support than women for Israeli military action, with no such gap for Hamas.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
The traits explained only 5 to 8 percent of the difference between people. Personality is a small part of this picture, not the main one, and the results do not say it outranks political orientation — only that both matter.

Everything is self-reported, on a topic where people shade answers to look acceptable. Both samples were non-representative internet users in Europe, with nobody from Israel or Gaza, so these are bystanders judging from far away. And it is one snapshot in time, so cause is unknown: a diet of violent news could shape the person as easily as the person shapes the answer. Anja Wertag, a researcher not involved in the work, warns against reading too much into it — backing violence on a questionnaire says nothing about who would actually do it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Ask most people whether violence is acceptable and they hear a different question: whose? For a few, that word was never in it.

recall.q: Across the samples, backing one side's violence usually meant rejecting the other's. So how could psychopathy and sadism predict more support for both at once?
recall.a: Because those two traits do not sort by side. Most people's answers follow the side they identify with, so support for one means less support for the other. Higher psychopathy and sadism came with a general acceptance of violence, which lifted support for both actors together, even after political orientation was accounted for.

cards.title: The brain may be two organs, not one
cards.body: Since the 1950s, biologists have assumed the whole brain grows from one kind of starter cell. A Stanford team now says there are two, split apart before the embryo even has a head or a tail: one road builds the thinking brain, the other builds the stalk that runs your breathing and your heartbeat. The same split shows up in animals that left our line 500 million years ago.
cards.evidence: single study · mouse embryos · gene expression, pattern checked in human, monkey, chicken, zebrafish, acorn worm

sections.text:
In the 1940s a farmer cut the head off a rooster named Mike and missed a piece. The cut spared the hindbrain — the brain stem, the stalk at the bottom of the skull. Mike lived another 18 months. Time magazine wrote about him in 1945.

That stalk runs your heartbeat, your breathing, your sleep and waking. In front of it sits the forebrain, which does memory, maths and poetry. Biologists have long treated the two as one organ with one beginning. In 1951 the Dutch embryologist Peter Nieuwkoop said the whole brain grows from a single kind of starter cell — a progenitor, meaning a cell already set on becoming brain and nothing else, but not yet on which part. The parts are joined, after all. A lung has two lobes and one origin; why not this?

A Stanford team led by Kyle Loh says it does not work that way. The difference sounds small. It changes everything after it. Old view: a cell becomes brain, then later picks which brain. New view: the moment a cell "puts on its brain hat", it has already picked a side — forebrain and midbrain down one road, hindbrain down the other. The same split turned up in monkeys, humans, chickens, zebrafish and acorn worms, which left our line more than 500 million years ago, before the continents gathered into Pangea.

Loh thinks the old picture is an accident of what we studied first. A jellyfish has two separate nervous systems at opposite ends of its body, and nobody calls that one organ. Look at a mouse or a human and you see one grey lump inside a skull, so you assume one source.

The practical half is sharper. Because everyone started from the wrong cell, nobody could grow hindbrain neurons in a dish — and the hindbrain is where a lot of medicine actually lands. Leptin, a drug aimed at the hypothalamus, the forebrain's energy-balance centre, never made humans lose weight. Ozempic works on hindbrain neurons instead. Destroy the ones it binds to in a mouse and the drug stops working, appetite and all. The nerves that move the face, jaw, tongue and throat sit there too. People with ALS, or with spinal muscular atrophy — the leading genetic killer of babies under one — often die because they can no longer swallow. Those cells can now be grown and studied.

Loh stops where his data stops. If two, why not three? He will not guess about the cerebellum, whose origin is unsettled, and the spinal cord may yet turn out to be a third source. Ask again in a year or two. He speculates about one thing only: why evolution would build this way. Separate sources buy freedom — you can change one part without touching the other. Evolution could play with the forebrain, adding memory and language, and never risk the circuits that keep the lungs moving. The thinking brain could afford to get strange because the living brain was not attached to the experiment.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: A mouse embryo at seven and a half days is a U-shaped clump of cells with no head or tail you can see. The team tracked which cells were switching on two genes, Otx2 and Gbx2. They did not find one pool of brain-starter cells. They found two, sitting in different places: the Otx2 group headed for forebrain and midbrain, the Gbx2 group for hindbrain. Researchers noticed in the 1990s that these genes switch on in different parts of the embryo. The new work goes further: the split is already there at the moment a cell commits to being brain.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one new paper in Nature Neuroscience against a model that has held since 1951, and the field pushed back hard — a department chair stood up at a conference and called it "completely false". The evidence is gene activity in early embryos, mostly mouse, with the pattern checked in five other animals. It is not proof that the two halves work as separate organs in an adult. Loh grants that the framing has a soft edge: everything in the body traces back to one fertilised egg, and look closely enough and any two things have two sources. His real claim is narrower, and it is about timing.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain that keeps you alive and the brain that writes the poem may never have been one organ — only two roads that ended up pressed together in the same skull.

recall.q: Both the old model and the new one agree that a cell can commit to becoming brain. So what do they disagree about?
recall.a: When the choice of which brain gets made. The old view said a brain starter cell was still undecided and could go on to make forebrain, midbrain or hindbrain. Loh's team found that the cell has already picked one track or the other at the very moment it commits to being brain at all.

cards.title: The brain keeps immune guard posts in the skull bone
cards.body: Scientists followed proteins out of a mouse's brain and found them arriving inside the skull bone. Waiting there were organised immune structures — the kind nobody had ever seen in healthy bone. Shut those structures down and brain tumours grew faster. Boost them with a gel under the scalp, and the mice fought their tumours off better and lived longer.
cards.evidence: single study · mouse model of glioblastoma · human skull marrow tissue only · published in Nature

sections.text:
A gel sits under the scalp of a mouse. It rests on the bone — not in the brain, not in the blood. Just three immune-boosting proteins against the skull. Inside, a brain tumour begins to lose. The mice that got the gel fought off their tumours better and lived longer than the ones that did not.

For a long time medicine treated the brain as sealed off from the immune system, the body's defence force. That idea has come apart, and Jonathan Kipnis's lab at WashU Medicine did much of the taking apart. First they found lymphatic vessels in the dura mater. The dura is the tough sheet of tissue just under the skull; lymphatic vessels are the drainage pipes the immune system patrols. Then they found tiny channels running through the skull bone itself — a direct road between brain and bone.

In the new study, published in Nature, they followed proteins along that road. The proteins left the brain, passed through the channels, and reached the marrow, the soft tissue inside the skull bone. Waiting there were organised immune structures that look like lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small command centres: T follicular helper cells push B cells to mass-produce antibodies, the proteins that tag an enemy for attack. Nobody had seen such structures in healthy bone marrow before. Nobody had found them inside bone at all.

Then the test. The team gave mice glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, and used a drug to shut the skull hubs down. Those tumours grew faster. Those mice died sooner. The structures were not decoration.

The gel was the other half of the argument. Its three proteins aimed at one thing: more antibodies, made right there in the skull marrow. Activity against the tumours surged. The detail that matters is the order — the response showed up first in the hubs inside the skull, and only later in the lymph nodes outside it. The defence starts at the door, not at headquarters.

Human skull marrow appears to hold similar immune cells, so this may not be a mouse-only arrangement. The prize, if it holds, is position. These hubs sit right against the brain, and you can reach them through the scalp. That raises a possibility: adjusting immune activity around the brain — in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, schizophrenia, long COVID, any illness with an immune side — without dosing the whole body. Kipnis calls the cells in the skull the brain's "first responders".

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is mouse work. The cancer was a mouse model of glioblastoma. The disrupting drug and the gel were tested in mice. Nothing here has been tried in a person. In human skull marrow the team found evidence of similar immune cells — a hint that we have the same arrangement, not proof that it does the same job. And a first-of-its-kind finding is exactly the kind that needs a second lab to see it too.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The bone around the brain was never only a wall. Something lives inside it, and it is on the brain's side.

recall.q: After the gel, the anti-tumour response showed up in two places. Why does the order in which they lit up matter?
recall.a: The activity appeared first in the hubs inside the skull bone marrow, and only later in the lymph nodes outside the skull. That order says the skull hubs are the brain's own first responders, not a late echo of the body's usual defence.

cards.title: Nigeria now refines its own petrol — prices rose anyway
cards.body: Nigeria's giant Dangote refinery raised its wholesale petrol price by 7% last week, and pumps in Lagos and Abuja followed. Local plants now make nearly 80% of the country's petrol, after years of relying on imports. It changed nothing: refining at home does not change what crude oil costs.

sections.text:
Pumps in Lagos and Abuja rose up to 5% after the refinery's 7% increase, and bigger jumps are expected in northern towns and rural areas. The refinery belongs to Aliko Dangote, Africa's richest man, and it has changed where Nigeria's fuel comes from: imports fell from 60% of supply last year to just over 20% between January and July.

That protected no one. Refining turns crude oil into petrol; it does not make the crude cheaper. Brent, the oil price Nigeria tracks, is up more than 70% since January and above $100 this month, pushed by the Iran war. Up to 40% of Dangote's crude is bought abroad at that world price.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 7% — Dangote's wholesale price rise; Lagos and Abuja pumps followed with up to 5%
80% — share of Nigeria's petrol made at home in the first half of 2026, against imports at just over 20%
70% — Brent crude's rise since January, to more than $100 a barrel
15.39% — Nigeria's inflation in August, barely down from July

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: President Tinubu ended Nigeria's decades-old fuel subsidy in 2023, and pump prices have risen five-fold since. Joe Ajaero, who leads a union of four million workers, warned this week of "incalculable damage" to wages, with a new school year and higher transport costs landing together. Tinubu wants a second term in January, and the cost of living is the campaign's main issue.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The central bank meets next week. August's slower inflation raised hopes of a rate cut, but analysts at CardinalStone expect no change, and Coronation Merchant Bank warns that energy costs staying high could slow disinflation — that is, inflation would come down more slowly than hoped. Dangote's shares went on sale Monday in Africa's largest stock market listing.

recall.q: Local plants now refine nearly 80% of Nigeria's petrol and imports have collapsed. So why did the pump price still jump?
recall.a: Refining only turns crude oil into petrol; it does not change what the crude itself costs. Brent is up more than 70% this year, and up to 40% of Dangote's crude is bought abroad at that world price, so the global shock passes straight through to Nigerian pumps.

cards.title: A US bill on Russia, and India's cheap oil problem
cards.body: The bill is aimed at Moscow. The pressure lands on New Delhi. Reuters reports that both of India's choices now cost something — and one of them shows up as fuel prices just before elections.

sections.text:
What does the bill do?

It is a new US sanctions bill on Russia, reported by Reuters on 18 September. It is written against Moscow. The part India feels is the threat of US tariffs — import taxes — on Indian exports.

Why is Delhi stuck?

Both doors cost money: tariffs would hit Indian exporters and sour the trade talks Delhi is already running with Washington. Carrying on with the Russian purchases could push fuel prices up at home, with elections close. Delhi's public answer is energy security — a country that large must be sure of its fuel.

What happens to the discounted Russian barrels?

Nobody has answered that. Delhi has not said it will stop buying. Washington has not said what it would accept.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Two things will settle it: what the final bill lets Washington do, and whether India's Russian purchases actually change. The trade talks are still open. Neither is public yet.

recall.q: The bill targets Russia. So why is India the one described as stuck?
recall.a: Because each of India's choices costs something. US tariffs would hit Indian exports and sour the trade talks with Washington. Carrying on with the Russian purchases is tied to higher fuel prices at home just before elections.

cards.title: Personality scores split Britain's parties into two groups
cards.body: Researchers asked 4,266 members of five British parties to agree or disagree with statements like "people who mess with me always regret it". Members who scored higher on narcissism, manipulation and coldness also preferred leaders described as having those traits — and no real politician was ever named. On average, Conservative and Reform UK members scored higher than Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green members.
cards.evidence: single study · n=4,266 party members · self-report surveys · UK only

sections.text:
"Group activities tend to be dull without me." That line sat on a survey form, waiting for a tick: agree or disagree. It went to 4,266 members of five British parties — Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens and Reform UK.

The statements measure three traits that psychologists group together and call the dark triad. Narcissism: a big view of yourself, a need to be admired, a habit of talking others down. Machiavellianism: cold, cynical, happy to use people, focused on power and money. Psychopathy: chasing thrills, charming on the surface, little feeling for others and little regret. The researchers are careful here. Nobody can be diagnosed from a survey form. Each score is a dial, not a label.

Now the guess. Which parties ticked agree more often — and which less?

There are good reasons to expect no gap at all. Joining any party is already an unusual thing to do. It takes a taste for argument and attention, wherever you sit. You might also expect the newest party to stand on its own, or the line to fall between the party in power and everyone else.

It fell somewhere else. Conservative and Reform UK members scored higher, on average, than Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green members. Five parties, two groups.

The second finding does the real work. The team also asked members what they liked in a leader — not by name, but by description. A leader who thinks they are special. One who will use people to get their way. One who is not bothered by hurting feelings. The higher a member's own score, the more they liked that kind of leader.

Why does that feel strange? Because we sort parties by what they believe. That is what the public argument is about, and earlier work on British party members took the same road: who they are, where they live, what they think. Personality was nearly a blank. This study suggests parties sort by personality too — what kind of person feels at home inside one, and what kind of leader appeals before a face is attached.

The authors read it as a personality version of something political scientists already describe: Britain as two camps rather than five parties. If few people cross between the camps, members may go easy on a close rival rather than help the other camp win.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
One study, and a survey at that. Asking people to rate their own vanity is a soft measure — you learn how they see themselves, not how they act. These are party members, not voters, and members are a small, odd slice of any party.

The gaps are averages across thousands of people. They say nothing about one member, and nothing about any real leader. And the link between a member's score and the leaders they like is only a link: the two move together, but the study cannot say which one shapes the other.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A party is not only a set of beliefs. It is also a room — and people choose the room where they feel normal.

recall.q: The researchers never named a real politician. What did they ask about instead, and why does that change what the finding means?
recall.a: They described leader traits in the abstract — a leader who thinks they are special, who will use people to get their way, who is not bothered by hurting feelings. Members who scored higher on those traits themselves preferred leaders described that way. So the match is about personality, not loyalty to a famous name.
